source.title: (tentatively) Found 600+ Monosemantic Features in a Small LM Using Sparse Autoencoders

record.tranche_reason: The post measures feature correspondence and interpretability across separately trained dictionaries, but it does not vary dictionary size or test splitting, absorption, feature hierarchies, or the sparsity-objective explanation.
record.gate_note: The post reports MCS and feature examples across independently trained dictionaries. These do not test the size-dependent splitting claim or any listed version. Other feature ablations and activation examples concern the interpretation of individual features, not splitting.
record.test_reason: The post trains SAEs on Pythia-70M layer 2 MLP and compares separately trained dictionaries by max cosine similarity and feature inspection. It does not vary dictionary size, and does not examine splitting, absorption, hierarchy or alternative objectives. It does not test any version. It does not even cite the splitting claim explicitly, so 'discusses' overstates it; it neither tests nor uses splitting (T6).
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The author tentatively claims 600+ meaningful features, e.g. a LaTeX '$' feature spanning many neurons, unlike neuron-basis features. Lower-MCS features look more polysemantic, yet some are meaningful. The author calls for more rigorous metrics and larger-model work.
record.recipe_differences: Uses sparse autoencoders on Pythia-70M layer_2 mid-MLP activations and compares feature vectors across separately trained dictionaries using MCS; it does not compare dictionary sizes or measure feature splitting.

fits_no_version.finding: Feature correspondence between separately trained dictionaries varies. High-MCS features looked interpretable; most low-MCS features were dead, but some low-MCS features seemed meaningful. The update says one dictionary found features another didn't.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: SAE features are only partly reproducible across training runs (seed/data), and low cross-run similarity does not imply a feature is meaningless.

record.problems: The post describes a quick inspection of the top 70 MCS features and says most low-MCS features could not be checked because they were dead. It does not report dictionary sizes or a quantitative test of splitting.
record.rows_left_out: Individual feature activation, context-ablation, logit-difference, and neuron-basis comparisons were left out because they concern interpretation or effects of individual features, not correspondence or splitting across dictionary sizes.

untested.parts: All; dictionary size is not varied.
All; only Pythia-70M layer 2 is studied, with the authors' own SAEs.
All; no feature families or hierarchy.
All; no cross-size decomposition. The update notes one dictionary found features another didn't, but these were same-setup runs, not different sizes.
All; no alternative objectives are compared.

record.verdict_notes: This is an early 2023 LessWrong post that predates the splitting literature. It has no dictionary-size comparison. Relation is changed from 'discusses' to 'cites_only'/T6, since splitting is never mentioned.

versions.untested_parts: Dictionary size is not varied; whether smaller features split into more specific features with covering inputs and nearby directions is not tested.
No scaling across large models or open SAE releases.
No nested feature families or hierarchy of concepts is tested.
Absorption and its response to SAE size or sparsity are not tested.
The dictionaries are not compared by size, and the post does not test decomposition of larger-SAE latents into smaller-SAE latents.
No alternative SAE objective, including Matryoshka SAEs, is tested.

rows.subject: Pythia-70M layer_2 mid-MLP (after the GeLU)
rows.operation_detail: Measured maximum cosine similarity (MCS) between feature vectors in separately trained dictionaries.
rows.measure: Maximum cosine similarity between feature vectors
rows.locator: Feature Case Study; Top-activating Examples for feature #52
rows.note: The post presents this as a high-MCS feature and interprets its examples as detecting LaTeX dollar signs. Dictionary sizes are not given or varied, so this does not establish size-dependent splitting.
rows.check: Selection value: the ~0.99 MCS was the criterion for choosing feature #52 for the case study, not a result on splitting. Dictionary sizes are not stated.

rows.subject: Pythia-70M layer_2 mid-MLP (after the GeLU)
rows.operation_detail: Inspected low-MCS features across separately trained dictionaries for activity and apparent meaning.
rows.measure: Feature activation count and qualitative interpretability
rows.value: Most low-MCS features checked were dead, with fewer than 10 activations and usually 0; feature 1580 appeared meaningful despite low MCS.
rows.note: The post says feature 1580 activates more after a meaningful word and affects the word after “rom”; it does not report dictionary sizes or whether this is a split.
rows.check: Qualitative inspection of low-MCS features across same-size, separately trained dictionaries (dead features; feature 1580). It has no bearing on size-dependent splitting.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
